items.title: 2.7.2 Distribution of electrons in subshells and orbitals: the Aufbau principle

source_refs.note: Topic 2.7.2, printed pages 34-36: the Aufbau principle, Table 2.6 and the energy order (Figure 2.12).

blocks.text: Three rules govern the filling of the orbitals of multi-electron atoms: the Aufbau principle, Pauli's exclusion principle and Hund's rule. The Aufbau or building-up principle states that the subshells of an atom are filled with electrons in increasing order of their energy. In the absence of a magnetic field the energy of a subshell depends on the principal quantum number n and the azimuthal quantum number l, so the order of filling can be obtained from the sum n + l.

blocks.caption: Values of n + l for the subshells (Table 2.6)

items: The subshell with the lower n + l value has the lower energy and is filled first. The 4s orbital has n + l = 4 + 0 = 4 and 3d has 3 + 2 = 5, so 4s has the lower energy and is filled before 3d.
If two subshells have equal n + l values, the one with the lower n is filled first. Both 4p (4 + 1 = 5) and 3d (3 + 2 = 5) have the value 5, and 3d is filled first because of its lower n.

blocks.text: By this rule the energy order of the subshells, and so the order of filling, is 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s.

blocks.alt: Left: boxes for the orbitals of each subshell stacked by energy from 1s at the bottom to 7s at the top, s in blue, p in orange, d in purple and f in green. Right: the Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules in words, a wrong and a right way of placing three electrons in three p boxes, and the box diagrams of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen.
blocks.caption: The energy order of the subshells and the three filling rules (original diagram after Figures 2.12 to 2.14 and Table 2.6).
blocks.long_description: Subshells fill from the bottom of the energy ladder: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, then 4s before 3d because its n + l is lower, then 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p and 7s. Pauli's principle allows two electrons per box only with opposite spins. Hund's rule puts electrons into the degenerate boxes of a subshell one at a time with parallel spins, so carbon's two 2p electrons and nitrogen's three sit in separate boxes, and only oxygen's fourth is forced to pair.
